leading_positions.synthesis: Four of eight members prefer B050 as their round-1 prize, all with the same trio (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), and the citation wording differs only slightly: Danielsson and Eriksson word the experimental half as the first observation or discovery in HgTe quantum wells, Olsson and Pearce use the generic wording. They share the view that the Z2 and quantum spin Hall prediction paired with a measurable quantised edge conductance is a sharp prediction confirmed by experiment, independently reproduced in transport and ARPES. They also share the same reservations, stated in each of the four files: the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and of the three-dimensional contributors, and overlap with the 2016 topological phases prize. They differ on fallbacks: Danielsson names a theory-only Kane-Mele prize, Eriksson names B051 or B002, Olsson raises whether the 2D effect or 3D topological insulators should anchor the citation, and Pearce names B051. Danielsson, Olsson and Pearce moved to B050 from different opening first choices (B003, B021 and B009), so this is a stated preference in round 1, not a count of earlier support.

Two members prefer optical lattice clocks with the two-name credit Katori and Ye, and both stress that it is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist. They share the argument that the magic-wavelength condition is a new principle that made neutral-atom ensembles competitive with single-ion clocks, and that Ye's group delivered the 1e-18 level and control of collective shifts. They agree that the citation must be written narrowly around the lattice clock, and that the pending SI redefinition of the second should not be a reason to wait. Both state that they carry field proximity, Kroll through a research stay in John Hall's laboratory and Lindroth as a theoretical atomic physicist. Both concede that overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes is the main objection, that ion-clock, ultrastable-laser and other lattice-clock contributors are uncredited, and that this ballot has the narrowest opening base of support. Both list B050 and B015 as alternatives.

One member prefers trapped-ion quantum computing with Cirac, Zoller and Blatt. The case rests on the 1995 Cirac-Zoller architecture and its realisation in Innsbruck, with high gate fidelities across several laboratories. Johansson himself identifies three weaknesses: the overlap with the 2012 ion-control prize, the contestability of Blatt as the experimental name versus Wineland, Monroe and others, and the lack of a demonstrated scalable machine. His response to Mehlig notes that B015 and B027 share Cirac and Zoller, so awarding one spends the same theory recognition. Johansson says he is recused from B038 and keeps it only as an alternative; he lists B038 and B050 as alternatives.

One member prefers quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, with Bloch, Cirac and Zoller. The argument is that a theoretical programme (Jaksch-Zoller, Cirac-Zoller) became a laboratory method confirmed by many groups, and that it changed how many-body problems are posed. Mehlig himself says the credit is not clean: five names are credited, Greiner and Dalibard are cut, and the committee's opening proposals disagreed on the third name. He also notes overlap with B015 through Cirac and Zoller and doubts whether analogue simulation has yet gone beyond classical simulability. He lists B015 and B002 as alternatives.

areas_of_agreement: All eight files treat B050, B051, B015 and B027 as scientifically serious, mature, independently reproduced candidates; the disagreements are about attribution, overlap with earlier prizes, and which criterion to weight, not about whether the physics holds.

Four members explicitly prefer B050, and the others who comment on it (Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig) describe it as a credible alternative they would not block, while keeping their own preference.

Every supporter of B050 names the same three credited laureates and the same two reservations (the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission and overlap with the 2016 prize), and Eriksson, Danielsson and Pearce each give a fallback if the attribution proves indefensible.

Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce agree in their files that the pending formal redefinition of the SI second should not by itself be a reason to delay a clock prize, and that if the committee prefers to wait it should say so explicitly.
Several members (Kroll, Lindroth, Eriksson) say any citation should be written narrowly around the specific achievement, so that it does not claim a whole field or the earlier prizes' territory.
scientific_disputes: Conceptual versus metrological criterion: Kroll states that B050 opened a new organising principle while the clock opened a new level of accuracy, and the committee has to decide which it ranks higher. Mehlig argues that lattice simulation changed how many-body problems are posed, while the clocks act on other physics mainly through tests and applications.

Whether lattice clocks are a distinct achievement or a refinement of the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion work: Kroll and Lindroth argue the magic-wavelength condition and many-atom statistics are a different principle; both acknowledge that a critic can read it as a very good refinement.

Whether B050 is distinct from the 2016 topological phases prize: the B050 supporters and Kroll (who agrees with Eriksson on this) treat Z2 classification with time-reversal symmetry as different, while Johansson and Mehlig say they remain unsure about the distance.

Whether the 2D quantum spin Hall effect or the 3D topological insulators should anchor B050: Olsson and Danielsson raise this, since three-dimensional materials arguably had larger impact but are not covered by the credited names.

Whether analogue quantum simulation has delivered results beyond classical simulability (Mehlig's own uncertainty) and whether trapped-ion computing is a computing architecture rather than physics (Johansson's own reservation) are both open; they share the Cirac-Zoller theory, but Johansson and Mehlig disagree on which is better bounded.
attribution_disputes: B050: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route Molenkamp realised and are outside the credited names, as are the 3D contributors (Fu, Moore, Balents, Hasan). Eriksson and Danielsson ask whether the BHZ omission undermines the experimental half; Johansson calls it a decisive theory contribution omitted, and Lindroth calls it a defect in the prize itself.

B051: the two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, but ion-clock groups, the ultrastable-laser work and other lattice-clock contributors (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Kimble are named by Lindroth) are uncredited.

B015: Blatt versus Wineland, Monroe, Home and Haeffner is, in Johansson's words, partly arbitrary, and the third slot is contestable; Kroll and Johansson also name Wineland's 2012 recognition as the overlap.

B027: five credited names are cut to three, and the committee's opening proposals disagree on whether the third name is Cirac, Greiner or Dalibard; Mehlig acknowledges Greiner and Dalibard would be unrecognised.
Cirac and Zoller are the theory originators in both B015 and B027, so whichever of the two is chosen effectively spends their recognition (raised by Johansson and Mehlig).
maturity_disputes: No member disputes the maturity of B050 or B051; Eriksson, Danielsson and Olsson cite roughly two decades of independent confirmation for B050, and Kroll and Lindroth cite replication in several laboratories and international comparisons for B051.
B051: whether the formal redefinition of the second should come first. Kroll and Lindroth say no; Pearce says the committee should decide this explicitly and not by default.

B015: Johansson and Lindroth note that scalable, error-corrected machines are not yet demonstrated, so a prize would honour enabling physics. Johansson argues that the foundational proposal and its first realisation is what the prize judges.
B027: Mehlig himself questions whether analogue simulation is yet a mature discovery or a promising programme.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson (Chalmers, directs WACQT) states he should be recused from B038 (circuit quantum electrodynamics) and its credit decision, and keeps it only as an alternative; he reports no specific conflict for B015.

Kroll discloses a research stay in John Hall's laboratory and field proximity to Jun Ye's JILA environment, with no documented personal or collaborative tie to Katori or Ye; he also notes closeness of his quantum-information work to the trapped-ion entry and says he would recuse if the committee judged these connections material.
Lindroth reports no conflict for Katori or Ye and describes her theoretical atomic physics field proximity as a source of bias rather than a formal conflict.

Olsson is a Chalmers colleague of Johansson, who ranks B038 first (Johansson himself now lists B015 as preferred and B038 as an alternative), reports no credited name at Chalmers, and notes a general academic exchange connection with Japan relevant to Katori (B051) but no personal one.
Eriksson reports field proximity through electronic-structure screening of topological materials and notes that he chaired the 2025 cycle; he reports no recusal issue.

Danielsson's field proximity is to inflation (B003), which he ranked first at opening and says he has discounted; Mehlig and Pearce report no specific conflict for the candidates they prefer (Pearce's astroparticle connections would have mattered only for B009, which he no longer proposes).
questions_for_round2: For B050: can the committee name a defensible reason for crediting Kane, Mele and Molenkamp while leaving out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang? If not, which of Mele or Molenkamp would a BHZ credit replace, and does that damage the experimental half of the citation, which Danielsson says a theory-only Kane-Mele prize would lose?

Does the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 classification count as a distinct achievement from the 2016 topological phases prize? Should the citation anchor on the 2D effect or on 3D topological insulators, as Olsson asks?

For B051: if the committee accepts the argument that the magic-wavelength lattice differs in principle from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion work, how should the citation be drafted to say so? Is the pending SI redefinition a reason to delay, and will the committee decide that explicitly?

Between B050 and B051, which criterion should decide: a new conceptual organising principle with a more complicated credit, or a metrological advance with a clean two-name credit? Will the members who ranked B051 or B015 first state whether they would accept B050 if the credit question were settled, and the reverse?

For B015 and B027, which share Cirac and Zoller: are these independent options? If the committee prefers one, who should take the experimental slot (Blatt, Bloch, Greiner or Dalibard), and how should the Wineland 2012 overlap be handled?

Do Kroll and Johansson wish the committee to treat their disclosed proximity to the clock and trapped-ion entries as material, and does Johansson's recusal from B038 need a formal note before B038 is discussed in round 2?
summary.chair_observation: In round 1 the stated preferences are 4 for B050, 2 for B051, 1 for B015 and 1 for B027. No member argues that the leading candidates lack scientific merit, so the open issues are attribution, overlap with earlier prizes, and which criterion to weight. The B050 group is the largest but its own members also name the credit problem as the main risk; the B051 group has a cleaner credit but a narrower base and the strongest overlap question. B015 and B027 each depend on the same Cirac and Zoller recognition. This summary counts only positions stated in the eight round-1 files and implies no hidden votes.
